Depuis quelques semaines, le Québec conn: For the past few weeks, Quebec has seen a surge of women who are survivors of sexual violence speaking out on social media and in the media.
Les violences sexuelles que subissent le: Sexual violence against women spares no community and no society. Yet on social media, as in the traditional media, it seems to have only one face – something racialized experts and survivors are denouncing.
Lorsque Sandra Boursiquot, une femme noi: When Sandra Boursiquot, a 46-year-old Black woman, publicly named her abuser Luis Miranda a few years ago, it became a widely covered case. Her experience, which she had tried in vain to report in 2009, was not made public until 2017. Today, she describes biased media coverage that helped discredit her and protect the abuser, who was in a position of power at the time. “They quoted the alleged accused without trying to get my side of the story,” she tells us in a Montréal café.
Mme Boursiquot affirme qu’elle a égaleme: Ms. Boursiquot says she also had great difficulty being heard by the authorities.
« Les policiers ont refusé de prendre ma: “The police refused to take my complaint,” she remembers. She was forced to turn to other resources for help before an investigator looked into her case. Casey Shakes, a Montréal filmmaker, is working on an Afrofuturist project inspired by her experience. In 2017, she decided to speak out and name her abuser. It was a gruelling step for this young Black woman, who has little trust in law enforcement. “Part of the trauma I experienced comes from my reluctance to report my abuser to the police,” says Casey.
Lorsqu’elle s’est présentée au poste de: When she first went to the police station, an officer reportedly told her there was nothing they could do because there was no physical evidence. He handed her the card of an organization, which she called. The worker she spoke to told her the authorities should have opened a file. After several months of legal steps and terror, she finally obtained a restraining order, a protection she says she had to fight hard to get. “My abuser reoffended and I had to call the police. At that point, the officers told me: ‘We can tell him to stop.’ I answered: ‘No, I want to file a complaint, I’ve had enough.’”
Le mouvement #MeToo a été fondé en 2006: The #MeToo movement was founded in 2006 by Tarana Burke, an African American activist. Drawing on her own experience, she wanted all victims of sexual violence to be heard. But 14 years later, things have not progressed enough. “We still see that the stories of people who don’t belong to the dominant group, meaning people who experience systemic forms of marginalization, are not taken into account and are not represented when we talk about the fight against sexual violence,” laments Marlihan Lopez, coordinator of the Simone de Beauvoir Institute at Concordia University.
Mme Lopez estime que les médias et les i: Ms. Lopez believes the media and institutions can contribute to the problem. “They play a role in producing myths and prejudices, and many communities don’t fit these images of a victim of sexual violence,” she explains. In her view, this means people from these communities are believed less and supported less.
« Au Québec, dans les médias, on met bea: “In Quebec, the media put a lot of emphasis on sexual violence when it involves people from the cultural world, who have a high profile. That’s a problem,” she laments. Kharoll-Ann Souffrant, a social worker pursuing a doctorate in social work at the University of Ottawa, makes similar remarks. Her thesis looks at sexual violence experienced by Black women in Quebec, as well as the #MeToo, #MoiAussi and #AggressionNonDénoncée movements. “Since 2017, we’ve seen the same issue with representation. In the United States as here, Black and marginalized communities are being erased.”
Selon cette dernière, la contribution du: According to Ms. Souffrant, the contribution of the Black Lives Matter movement means the issue is being discussed more in 2020. She says speaking out is not an option for many women, particularly those who have difficult relationships with the police. She attributes this reality to the police brutality and racial profiling experienced by Black and racialized people. “It isolates victims, who can’t speak easily,” says the University of Ottawa doctoral candidate.
« Lorsqu’il est question de violences se: “When it comes to sexual violence, it’s hard to be believed, and it’s even harder for a Black, racialized or Indigenous person,” Ms. Souffrant continues. One cause of this phenomenon could be a problem of representation, since these women don’t always match the image some people have of a victim.
« Il y a beaucoup de méfiance et de juge: “There is a lot of mistrust and judgment, and it comes partly from the prejudices we hold about these people. Stereotypes, whether or not they are unconsciously internalized, are projected onto these marginalized women who speak out,” she explains. According to Ms. Souffrant, the homogeneity seen in the media and across various institutions may have something to do with it. “Traditional media are run by white people. That means there are blind spots in their considerations.
Certaines choses sont évidentes pour nou: Some things are obvious to us because we live them, but they don’t match their reality. The lack of diversity in front of and behind the camera can explain these dynamics.”
Elle observe en outre que les femmes noi: She also observes that Black, Indigenous and marginalized women are not represented in public policy in Canada and Quebec either, and that they are forgotten in government strategies.
Comme le soulignent les expertes, beauco: As the experts point out, many women remain invisible when it comes to sexual violence, including sex workers, people from LGBTQ+ communities and people with disabilities. “The different systems of oppression – like sexism, racism, homophobia and transphobia – really create barriers,” sums up Ms. Souffrant. “It is really hard for these people to speak out and get help.” These barriers are also obstacles when it comes to the services offered to victims.
Tarah Paul est chargée de projet au Cent: Tarah Paul is a project manager at the Centre d’aide et de lutte contre les agressions à caractère sexuel (CALACS) de l’Ouest-de-l’Île, an organization that offers a free, confidential support service to girls and women who are victims of sexual assault. She is currently working on a project called Adaptons nos pratiques à la diversité des survivantes, which aims to start a dialogue on how community organizations can become more accessible and more inclusive by creating a safe environment for all women, whether they are Black, Indigenous, racialized, living with a disability, LGBTQ+ or have precarious immigration status.
« Les ressources d’aide ne sont pas touj: “Support resources are not always accessible or welcoming, and don’t necessarily meet their needs,” she observes. “This is the time for all community organizations to have a discussion by asking themselves: ‘Is there a way to improve our services to make them safer and more inclusive?’ We need to analyze the services we offer and ask ourselves whether they are adequate. We also need to question our intervention practices, and more,” she stresses. Ms. Paul thinks funding should be allocated to specialized organizations that serve marginalized communities so they can help victims of sexual violence.
Selon Marlihan Lopez, plusieurs initiati: According to Marlihan Lopez, many initiatives suffer from a lack of funding.
La Coalition pour le définancement de la: The Defund the Police Coalition, for one, proposes that funds paid to the SPVM be redirected to organizations that help victims. “We have neighbourhoods like Montréal-Nord where there is an increased police presence, but no services for violence,” she says. Ms. Lopez also points out that sex education is important too. “If we don’t have an education that allows us to address sexual violence in an inclusive way, that’s a problem,” she says. “We need to create awareness programs that are inclusive and that represent the realities of the different communities facing sexual violence.”
Kharoll-Ann Souffrant abonde dans ce sen: Kharoll-Ann Souffrant agrees and takes the thinking further.
« Les écoles primaires et secondaires, à: “Elementary and high schools, unlike post-secondary institutions, have no protocol to prevent and address the sexual violence children may experience,” she notes. “When there is no protocol, there is a risk that victims won’t be taken seriously, that their problem won’t be dealt with, or that the way they are helped will victimize them again. Staff need to be trained on this,” says Ms. Souffrant.
« Il faut être à l’écoute de la victime: “You have to listen to the victim and support her, listen to her needs,” explains Ms. Souffrant. “To do that, you can ask her: ‘What can I do for you? How can I support you?’” concludes the social worker.
